label: Information Overload
framing: We were promised that more information would make us wise. It has mostly made us anxious. Scripture never equates knowing more with knowing well, and it warns that the heart, not the feed, is what must be guarded, since from it flow the springs of life.
cultural: We carry in our pocket more news of the world's pain than any generation could hold, refreshed every hour, and we mistake the ache it produces for engagement. The feed is built to keep us scrolling, not to leave us settled, and we have confused being informed with being formed.
historical: Long before the smartphone, the desert fathers fled the noise of the city to find a word from God in silence. Pascal wrote in the seventeenth century that all of humanity's troubles come from our inability to sit quietly in a room alone, and Neil Postman warned in the 1980s that a culture drowning in information would slowly amuse and distract itself past the capacity for serious thought.
application: Choose your inputs the way you choose your food, since you become what you take in. Set hours when the feed is closed and the room is quiet, and let your mind learn stillness again. Read one thing slowly and to the end rather than ten things halfway. And carry the world's real griefs to God in prayer rather than letting the scroll leave you informed, agitated, and unable to act.

verses.text: All things are wearisome, more than one can describe; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing.
verses.where: At the start of his search the Teacher says all things are wearisome, more than one can describe: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing. The site's note on the chapter says he set out to explore everything done under heaven and found wisdom itself a source of grief. The appetite for more to see and hear is old, and it has never been satisfied by more.

verses.text: And by these, my son, be further warned: There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body.
verses.where: The book's closing voice praises the Teacher's careful work and then warns that there is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body. The site's note says this frame narrator gives the conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments. More words are not the same as wisdom, and the book ends by pointing past all of them to God.

verses.text: Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life.
verses.where: A father urges his son to guard his heart with all diligence, for from it flow the springs of life, and, as the site's note says, to guard his speech, his eyes and his steps as well. The site's note on the chapter explains that in Hebrew thought the heart is the place of thinking, deciding, remembering and desiring. What a person lets in shapes all of that.

verses.text: Others are like the seeds sown among the thorns. They hear the word, but the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.
verses.where: In the parable of the sower, the seed among thorns is heard, but the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth and the desire for other things come in and choke it. The site's note says none of the three is described as scandalous sin; all are ordinary. The plain note asks whether a life has become too full to give the word room.

verses.text: Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, or set foot on the path of sinners, or sit in the seat of mockers. But his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night.
verses.where: The first psalm blesses the person who does not take the counsel of the wicked or sit with mockers, but whose delight is in the law of the LORD, meditating on it day and night. The site's plain note asks where drifting has become sitting, and suggests reading a few lines of Scripture slowly and returning to them during the day. To meditate is to let a few words go deep, the opposite of taking in many quickly.

verses.text: Now about food sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.
verses.where: Writing about food offered to idols, Paul agrees with the Corinthians' knowledge and then says knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. The site's note says knowledge without love can destroy a fellow believer, and the plain note asks when being right has mattered more than the person in front of us. Knowing more about everything does not make anyone more loving.

verses.text: Now all the Athenians and foreigners who lived there spent their time doing nothing more than hearing and articulating new ideas.
verses.where: Luke remarks that the Athenians and foreigners in the city spent their time doing nothing but hearing and talking about new ideas. The site's plain note says Paul, troubled by what the city worshipped, went to talk with people rather than away from them. A life spent on the newest thing can leave no room for the one thing that matters.

verses.text: Then the LORD said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the LORD. Behold, the LORD is about to pass by.” And a great and mighty wind tore into the mountains and shattered the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire came a still, small voice.
verses.where: At Horeb the LORD passes by, and he is not in the great wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in a still, small voice. The site's note on the chapter tells how God then answered Elijah's complaint with new work. God is often not found in the loudest thing, and a mind full of noise can miss what is quiet.

verses.text: For the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, has said: “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence— but you were not willing.”
verses.where: When Judah's leaders sent envoys and treasure to Egypt without asking God, he told them their strength would lie in repentance, rest and quiet confidence, but they were not willing. The site's note says he still longs to be gracious and will answer their cry. Quiet in Scripture is not idleness; it is trust that does not need to rush toward every source of help.

verses.text: And this is my prayer: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight, so that you may be able to test and prove what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
verses.where: Paul prays that the Philippians' love will abound in knowledge and depth of insight, so that they may test and approve what is best. The site's plain note asks the reader to pray this for someone they love: not only that their troubles end, but that their love grows wiser. The aim of knowing is discernment and love, not more knowing.

links.label: Practical guides for life in the world

misread.taken: The eye is the lamp of the body is often quoted as if it were only a rule about what to watch, a verse for screens and nothing else.
misread.says: The site's note says that in context the saying stands between Jesus' words on treasure and on masters, and concerns how a person looks at money: the generous eye fills life with light, the grasping eye darkens it. The same note sets out an ancient picture of the eye as a lamp shining from the body's inner light. Applying it to what we watch is not wrong, but the verse asks first what the heart is fixed on, and greed can darken a life as surely as anything on a screen.
misread.text: The eye is the lamp of the body. If your eyes are good, your whole body will be full of light.

whole: Many people end the day having read a hundred headlines, a dozen arguments, several crises and countless opinions, and feel more tired and less sure of anything than when they began. The phone is checked before the eyes are fully open and again in the last minutes before sleep. Attention slips from one thing to the next, and it becomes hard to read a long page, sit through a conversation, or pray for more than a minute. It feels like being informed. Often it is closer to being flooded: knowing a little about everything, and having no time left to know anything, or anyone, well.

Scripture saw the hunger underneath long before the feeds. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, the Teacher says, nor the ear with hearing, and there is no end to the making of many books. The Athenians spent their time on nothing but new ideas. Paul warned that knowledge puffs up while love builds up. The Bible does not despise learning; it praises the discerning heart that seeks knowledge. But it knows that more information does not make a person wiser, and that what we take in shapes the heart, the place of thinking, deciding and desiring. Some of our overload is fear of missing something, some is restlessness, some is a way to avoid silence, and all of us have reached for the phone to avoid sitting with a thought, a person or God.

So the Bible's wisdom is to guard the heart and to choose what goes into it. Meditate on a few true words rather than skimming many, as Psalm 1 says. Keep times and places without the flood: the first minutes of the morning, the table, the last hour before sleep, one day in seven. Notice what leaves you more loving and what leaves you puffed up, anxious or numb, and take less of the second. Read something long and slow. Listen for the still, small voice, which is easy to miss when everything else is loud. And pray, as Paul did, for love that grows in knowledge and insight, so that you can tell what is best rather than only what is new.

The hope Scripture gives is that you do not need to know everything, because God does. His strength for his people lay in quiet confidence, not in rushing toward every source of help. The conclusion of the book that warns about many books is short: fear God and keep his commandments. A life rooted near the water, the first psalm says, bears fruit in season. There is more to hear than any person can take in, and you are free not to try.
deep.sit: What do you reach for when there is a quiet moment, and what might you hear if you let one of those moments stay quiet?

prayer.lead: A short song of a soul that has stopped reaching for things too great for it. The site's plain note says it does not say those things do not matter; it says you can be quiet with God while they wait.
prayer.text: My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty. I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me. O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore.
